newsitem.title: USA: Court revives U.S. investor suit against Lloyd's.
newsitem.headline: Court revives U.S. investor suit against Lloyd's.

text.p: A federal appeals court revived a lawsuit by U.S. investors in Lloyd's of London, clearing the way for a trial against Lloyd's in U.S. federal court, attorneys for the investors said on Friday.
The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco, in an opinion issued Thursday, reversed a lower court's decision to dismiss the federal claims brought by the investors.
The appeals court, however, upheld the decision of the district court to dismiss breach of fiduciary duty and certain state securities fraud claims against Lloyd's.
The Lloyd's investors, known as Names, said the appeals court decision would pave the way for a full trial on the merits of the case in federal court in San Diego, Calif.

"This decision of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals will finally allow U.S. Names to commence discovery and present their overwhelming evidence of Lloyd's fraudulent acts," Richard Rosenblatt, chairman of the American Names Association, charged in a statement.
Lloyd's of London said the decision ran counter to several other rulings on similar issues, adding it planned to appeal.

"We think the decision is erroneous and we plan to take steps to have it reversed," Lloyd's spokesman William Pitt said. He said attorneys for Lloyd's of London were likely to ask the appeals court to reconsider its decision.
Between 1970 and 1993, Lloyd's recruited 3,196 Names in the United States and raised $600 million from them.
In 1994, several hundred American Names sued Lloyd's in U.S. federal court for securities fraud and other claims. They alleged that Lloyd's pushed large liabilities on them without full disclosure.

In 1995, the district court hearing the case dismissed the complaint. In its decision, the district court held that the remedies available in Britain were sufficient to protect the American investors. It also ruled that there was not enough evidence to support allegations that certain Lloyd's agreements with the Names were obtained by fraud.
In Thursday's decision, the appeals court reversed the district court's dismissal of the Names' federal securities claims. The appeals court also reversed dismissal of the racketeering claims.
However, the appeals court said the judgement of the district court was affirmed in its dismissal of state securities fraud, common law fraud and breach of fiduciary duty claims.
Last year, nearly 95 percent of Names worldwide accepted a litigation settlement offer from Lloyd's.
"Only a very small number of Names remain involved in litigation of any kind," Pitt said.
